title: The Gold Standard: Randomized Experiments & Potential Outcomes
text:
Welcome to STAT 579! This week, we begin our journey by establishing the fundamental principles of causal inference. Our goal is to move beyond mere association (“A is correlated with B”) to make credible claims about causation (“A causes B”). To do this, we need a precise language and a rigorous framework.
This module introduces the Potential Outcomes framework, which is the bedrock of modern causal inference. We will then explore why the Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) is considered the “gold standard” design for answering causal questions and how it elegantly solves the most significant challenge in the field.


By the end of this week, you will be able to:

Define a causal effect for an individual and a population using the Potential Outcomes framework.
Explain the “Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference” and its implications.
Articulate the two components of the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA) and identify potential violations.
Prove why randomization allows the difference-in-means to be an unbiased estimator of the Average Treatment Effect (ATE).
Calculate an estimated ATE from data and connect it to the output of both a t-test and a simple linear regression model in R.

title: The Gold Standard: Randomized Experiments & Potential Outcomes
section: Part 1: The Language of Causality (Tuesday Session)
text:
Part 1: The Language of Causality (Tuesday Session)

The Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference
The central challenge of causal inference can be stated simply: we can never observe an individual’s outcome under both treatment and control at the same time. For any person, we see what happened, but we can never see what would have happened under a different choice. This unobservable outcome is known as the counterfactual.
Causal inference, therefore, is a scientific approach to dealing with a missing data problem. For every individual, at least one potential outcome is missing.


🧠 Clarifying The Concept: The Two Paths Analogy

Imagine you are a doctor with a patient who has high blood pressure. You stand at a fork in the road for their treatment plan. Path A is to prescribe a new drug. Path B is to prescribe a placebo. You can only choose one path. If you choose the drug (Path A), you will observe their blood pressure in a month. But you will never know what their blood pressure would have been had you chosen the placebo (Path B) at that same moment. That un-chosen path represents the counterfactual. The core task of causal inference is to find rigorous ways to compare the destinations of Path A and Path B, even though no single patient can ever travel both.



The Potential Outcomes Framework
To reason about these two paths, we use the Potential Outcomes framework (also called the Neyman-Rubin Causal Model). Let’s establish our notation for a simple scenario with a binary treatment.

Unit \(i\): An individual in our study (e.g., a patient, a person, a school).
Treatment \(Z_i\): A binary variable, where \(Z_i=1\) if unit \(i\) receives the treatment and \(Z_i=0\) if unit \(i\) receives the control.
Potential Outcomes \(Y_i(1)\) and \(Y_i(0)\): These are the pre-existing, latent outcomes for unit \(i\) under both possible scenarios.

\(Y_i(1)\): The outcome for unit \(i\) if they were to receive the treatment (\(Z=1\)).
\(Y_i(0)\): The outcome for unit \(i\) if they were to receive the control (\(Z=0\)).


For any given individual, both \(Y_i(1)\) and \(Y_i(0)\) are assumed to exist before any treatment is actually assigned.


The Individual Causal Effect (\(\tau_i\))
The individual causal effect (\(\tau_i\), or “tau”) is the difference between these two potential outcomes for a single unit:
\[
\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)
\]
Because of the Fundamental Problem, we can never observe \(\tau_i\) for any individual. We can only observe one of the two potential outcomes. The observed outcome, \(Y_i\), is linked to the potential outcomes through the treatment assignment \(Z_i\):
\[
Y_i = Z_i \cdot Y_i(1) + (1-Z_i) \cdot Y_i(0)
\]
This is a compact way to say that if \(Z_i=1\), we observe \(Y_i(1)\); if \(Z_i=0\), we observe \(Y_i(0)\).


✅ Example: A Hypothetical Drug Trial (“God’s-eye View”)
Let’s test a new blood pressure drug on 6 patients. Imagine we have a “God’s-eye view” and can see all potential outcomes (in mmHg).

From this complete data, we can see the true causal effect for each person. But in reality, we can’t see this full table.


From Individuals to Populations: The Average Treatment Effect (ATE)
Since we cannot access \(\tau_i\), we shift our goal to a more feasible target: the Average Treatment Effect (ATE). The ATE is the average of the individual causal effects across our population of interest.
\[
\text{ATE} = E[\tau_i] = E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)]
\]
By the linearity of expectation, a fundamental rule in probability, we can rewrite this as:
\[
\text{ATE} = E[Y_i(1)] - E[Y_i(0)]
\]
Using our “God’s-eye view” data, the true ATE is:

\(E[Y(1)] = (130 + 125 + 140 + 135 + 150 + 140) / 6 = 136.67\)
\(E[Y(0)] = (145 + 130 + 150 + 155 + 155 + 145) / 6 = 146.67\)
True ATE = \(136.67 - 146.67 = \mathbf{-10.0}\) mmHg



📌 Key Assumption: SUTVA
The entire Potential Outcomes framework rests on the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA). This is a crucial assumption we make in almost all causal analyses. SUTVA has two parts:

No Interference: The potential outcomes for one unit are unaffected by the treatment assignment of other units.

Public Health Example: In a vaccine trial, if vaccinating person A reduces the chance that person B (in the placebo group) gets the flu, then person B’s outcome has been “interfered” with by person A’s treatment. This violates the no-interference assumption. These are often called “spillover” effects.

Consistency (or “One Version of Treatment”): For a unit \(i\) who received treatment \(Z_i=z\), their observed outcome \(Y_i\) is equal to their potential outcome \(Y_i(z)\). This implies that there is only one “version” of the treatment.

Public Health Example: A therapy program is the “treatment.” If some therapists are far more effective than others, then a patient’s outcome depends not just on getting therapy (\(Z=1\)), but on which therapist they got. In this case, there are multiple versions of the treatment, and the consistency assumption may be violated.

Part 2: The Power of Randomization (Thursday Session)

From “God’s-eye View” To Reality
In a real study, we must assign treatments. Suppose we randomly assign patients 1, 3, 5 to the drug (\(Z=1\)) and patients 2, 4, 6 to the placebo (\(Z=0\)). The data we actually collect would look like this:

Selection Bias: The Arch-Nemesis of Causal Inference
The simplest way to estimate the effect is to compare the average outcomes in the two groups. But is this comparison valid? Let’s decompose the “naïve” difference in means:
\[
\underbrace{E[Y | Z=1] - E[Y | Z=0]}_{\text{Naïve Difference}} = \underbrace{E[Y(1) | Z=1] - E[Y(0) | Z=0]}_{\text{What we can calculate}}
\]
Through a small algebraic trick (see Appendix), we can rewrite this as:
\[
\text{Naïve Difference} = \underbrace{E[Y(1) - Y(0) | Z=1]}_{\text{ATT}} + \underbrace{\{E[Y(0) | Z=1] - E[Y(0) | Z=0]\}}_{\text{Selection Bias}}
\]
where ATT is the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated.






Selection Bias



Selection Bias is the systematic difference in baseline potential outcomes (\(Y(0)\)) between the group that receives treatment and the group that does not. In observational studies, this is almost always present. For example, sicker patients may be more likely to seek out a new treatment, meaning the treated group was less healthy to begin with. This bias will distort our estimate of the causal effect.




Randomization To the Rescue
This is where the magic of the Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) comes in. By randomly assigning the treatment \(Z\), we sever any systematic link between the treatment and the potential outcomes. On average, the group that gets the treatment is identical to the group that gets the control on all baseline characteristics, both observed and unobserved.






Theorem: Independence by Randomization



In an ideal RCT, the treatment assignment \(Z\) is statistically independent of the potential outcomes \((Y(1), Y(0))\). We write this as:
\[
(Y(1), Y(0)) \perp Z
\]
This implies that the expectation of a potential outcome is the same regardless of which group you look at:

\(E[Y(0) | Z=1] = E[Y(0) | Z=0] = E[Y(0)]\)
\(E[Y(1) | Z=1] = E[Y(1) | Z=0] = E[Y(1)]\)



Because of this property, the selection bias term becomes zero:
\[
\text{Selection Bias} = E[Y(0) | Z=1] - E[Y(0) | Z=0] = 0
\]
And our decomposition simplifies beautifully:
\[
E[Y | Z=1] - E[Y | Z=0] = E[Y(1)] - E[Y(0)] = \text{ATE}
\]
This proves that in an RCT, the simple difference in observed means is an unbiased estimator of the Average Treatment Effect.


Estimation And Lab Preview
Our estimator for the ATE, denoted \(\hat{\tau}_{ATE}\), is the sample difference-in-means:
\[
\hat{\tau}_{ATE} = \bar{Y}_{Z=1} - \bar{Y}_{Z=0}
\]
✅ Example: Estimating the ATE from Observed Data
Using our observed data:

Treated Group (\(Z=1\)): {130, 140, 150}. Mean \(\bar{Y}_1 = 140.0\).
Control Group (\(Z=0\)): {130, 155, 145}. Mean \(\bar{Y}_0 = 143.33\).

Our estimate is:
\[
\hat{\tau}_{ATE} = 140.0 - 143.33 = \mathbf{-3.33} \text{ mmHg}
\]
This estimate (-3.33) differs from the true ATE (-10.0) due to random sampling variability. Because our sample is tiny, this one particular randomization wasn’t perfectly balanced. However, the procedure is unbiased, meaning if we repeated this experiment many times, the average of our estimates would converge to the true value.
In our lab session, we will perform these calculations in R.
# Data from our example
df <- data.frame(
  sbp = c(130, 140, 150, 130, 155, 145),
  treatment = c(1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0)
)

# 1. Manual difference-in-means
mean_treated <- mean(df$sbp[df$treatment == 1])
mean_control <- mean(df$sbp[df$treatment == 0])
ate_est <- mean_treated - mean_control
print(ate_est)
#> [1] -3.333333

# 2. Using a t-test (standard statistical procedure)
t.test(sbp ~ treatment, data = df, var.equal = TRUE)
# The output provides the means of both groups and the difference.

# 3. Using a linear model (regression)
model <- lm(sbp ~ treatment, data = df)
summary(model)
# The coefficient for 'treatment' is our ATE estimate!


❓ Check Your Understanding

Question: A study on a new tutoring program allows students to sign up voluntarily. Researchers find that tutored students have higher test scores. Why is this likely not a pure causal effect? What is the likely direction of the selection bias?


Answer

This is an observational study, not an RCT. Students who voluntarily sign up for tutoring are likely more motivated or have more parental support than those who do not. This means their baseline potential outcome, \(E[Y(0) | Z=1]\) (what their score would have been without tutoring), is likely higher than the baseline for the non-tutored group, \(E[Y(0) | Z=0]\). This is positive selection bias, which makes the tutoring program appear more effective than it truly is.



2. Question: In a study of a new fertilizer on corn fields, some fields are very large and some are small. The “treatment” is a uniform application rate (e.g., 10kg per hectare). Does this scenario potentially violate any part of SUTVA?


Answer

This could violate the Consistency assumption (“one version of the treatment”). While the application rate is the same, the actual farming practices, soil quality, and other factors might differ systematically between large and small fields. If the effect of the fertilizer depends on these other factors that are bundled with the unit type, one might argue there are different “versions” of how the treatment is experienced. There is no interference mentioned.

title: The Gold Standard: Randomized Experiments & Potential Outcomes
section: 📚 Appendix: Advanced Statistical Derivations and Theory
text:
📚 Appendix: Advanced Statistical Derivations and Theory

📕 Topic 1: Formal Proof of Unbiasedness of the ATE Estimator
Motivation: Proving that our estimator is “unbiased” is the theoretical guarantee that our estimation procedure, on average, will give us the right answer. It is the foundation for all valid inference in an RCT.
Derivation: We want to show that \(E[\hat{\tau}_{ATE}] = \text{ATE}\). The estimator is \(\hat{\tau}_{ATE} = \bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_0\). By linearity of expectation, \(E[\hat{\tau}_{ATE}] = E[\bar{Y}_1] - E[\bar{Y}_0]\). Let’s analyze \(E[\bar{Y}_1] = E[Y_i | Z_i=1]\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
E[Y_i | Z_i=1] &= E[Z_i Y_i(1) + (1-Z_i)Y_i(0) | Z_i=1] & & \text{1. Substitute for } Y_i \
&= E[1 \cdot Y_i(1) + (1-1)Y_i(0) | Z_i=1] & & \text{2. Plug in } Z_i=1 \
&= E[Y_i(1) | Z_i=1] & & \text{3. Simplify} \
&= E[Y_i(1)] & & \text{4. By independence from randomization}
\end{aligned}
\]
Similarly, \(E[\bar{Y}_0] = E[Y_i | Z_i=0] = E[Y_i(0)]\). Therefore, \[
E[\hat{\tau}_{ATE}] = E[Y_i(1)] - E[Y_i(0)] = \text{ATE}
\]
The proof is complete. The key step (4) relies entirely on randomization making treatment assignment independent of potential outcomes.


📕 Topic 2: Variance of the ATE Estimator
Motivation: Unbiasedness tells us our aim is correct, but variance tells us about our precision. We need the variance to calculate standard errors and confidence intervals, which communicate the uncertainty in our estimate.
Derivation: The variance of our estimator is \(Var(\hat{\tau}_{ATE}) = Var(\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_0)\). Because the treatment and control groups are independent samples, the variance of the difference is the sum of the variances:
\[
Var(\hat{\tau}_{ATE}) = Var(\bar{Y}_1) + Var(\bar{Y}_0)
\]
For the sample mean of the treated group, \(Var(\bar{Y}_1) = \frac{Var(Y_i | Z_i=1)}{n_1} = \frac{\sigma^2_1}{n_1}\). Similarly, \(Var(\bar{Y}_0) = \frac{\sigma^2_0}{n_0}\).
So, the true variance of the estimator is:
\[
Var(\hat{\tau}_{ATE}) = \frac{\sigma^2_1}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma^2_0}{n_0}
\]
In practice, we don’t know the true population variances \(\sigma^2_1\) and \(\sigma^2_0\). We estimate them using the sample variances from our data, \(S^2_1\) and \(S^2_0\). The estimated variance is: \[
\widehat{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{ATE}) = \frac{S^2_1}{n_1} + \frac{S^2_0}{n_0}
\]
The Standard Error (SE) is the square root of this estimated variance: \(SE(\hat{\tau}_{ATE}) = \sqrt{\frac{S^2_1}{n_1} + \frac{S^2_0}{n_0}}\).
✅ Worked Example:
From our observed data:

Treated Group {130, 140, 150}: \(n_1=3\), Sample Variance \(S^2_1 = \frac{(130-140)^2 + (140-140)^2 + (150-140)^2}{3-1} = 100\).
Control Group {130, 155, 145}: \(n_0=3\), Sample Variance \(S^2_0 = \frac{(130-143.33)^2 + (155-143.33)^2 + (145-143.33)^2}{3-1} \approx 175\).

\(\widehat{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{ATE}) = \frac{100}{3} + \frac{175}{3} \approx 33.33 + 58.33 = 91.66\)
\(SE(\hat{\tau}_{ATE}) = \sqrt{91.66} \approx \mathbf{9.57}\)


📕 Topic 3: Equivalence of Difference-in-Means and Simple Regression
Motivation: This proof provides a critical link between the simple, non-parametric approach of comparing means and the more flexible framework of linear regression. It shows that for the simplest case, they are identical, justifying our use of regression to estimate causal effects.
Derivation: Consider the simple linear regression model \(Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Z_i + \epsilon_i\), where \(Z_i \in {0, 1}\). The OLS estimator for \(\beta_1\) is \(\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{Cov(Z, Y)}{Var(Z)}\). Let \(p = n_1/N\) be the proportion treated.

Variance of Z: \(Var(Z) = E[Z^2] - (E[Z])^2 = p - p^2 = p(1-p)\).
Covariance of Z and Y: \(Cov(Z, Y) = E[ZY] - E[Z]E[Y]\).
\(E[ZY] = E[Y|Z=1]P(Z=1) + E[Y|Z=0]P(Z=0) = \bar{Y}_1 \cdot p + \bar{Y}_0 \cdot 0 = p\bar{Y}_1\).
\(E[Y] = \bar{Y}_1 \cdot p + \bar{Y}_0 \cdot (1-p)\).
\(Cov(Z, Y) = p\bar{Y}_1 - p(\bar{Y}_1 p + \bar{Y}_0 (1-p)) = p\bar{Y}_1 - p^2\bar{Y}_1 - p(1-p)\bar{Y}_0 = p(1-p)\bar{Y}_1 - p(1-p)\bar{Y}_0 = p(1-p)(\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_0)\).

Now, we compute the ratio:
\[
\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{p(1-p)(\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_0)}{p(1-p)} = \bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_0
\]
This shows that the OLS estimate of the slope coefficient for a binary regressor is exactly the difference in the sample means between the group where \(Z=1\) and the group where \(Z=0\).

title: Week 6: Propensity Score Methods (Revised)
text:
In a perfect world, we would answer all causal questions using a Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT). By randomly assigning treatment, we ensure that, on average, the treated and control groups are identical on all background characteristics (both observed and unobserved). Any difference in their outcomes can therefore be attributed to the treatment.
However, in public health and clinical research, RCTs are often unethical, impractical, or too expensive. We must rely on observational data, where individuals select their own treatments. This leads to a critical problem: people who choose treatment are often systematically different from those who do not.
This week, we introduce propensity score methods, a powerful toolkit designed to address this selection bias. Propensity scores allow us to mimic the properties of an RCT by creating balanced comparison groups, helping us to isolate the causal effect of a treatment from the confounding effects of other variables.
By the end of this module, you will be able to:

Define the propensity score and explain its central role in causal inference.
Understand and explain the balancing property of the propensity score and why it is crucial for creating comparable groups.
Estimate propensity scores using logistic regression and other methods.
Implement three core propensity score methods: matching, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), and stratification.
Assess whether a propensity score model has successfully balanced the covariates between the treated and control groups using diagnostic plots and tables.
Critically evaluate the advantages and limitations of propensity score methods and their underlying assumptions.






Imagine we want to know the effect of a new fitness program (treatment D=1) on weight loss (outcome Y). In our observational data, people who joined the program lost more weight. But can we conclude the program caused the weight loss?
Probably not. The people who chose to join are likely different. They might be younger, more health-conscious, or have better access to healthy food. This is confounding. We are comparing a group of motivated “apples” to a general population of “oranges.”
The goal of propensity scores is to solve this problem by creating a “handicap” system. Instead of trying to match people on dozens of characteristics (age, gender, income, diet, etc.), we can boil all of that information down into a single number: the propensity score.




The propensity score is the probability that a unit (e.g., a person) receives the treatment, given their observed baseline covariates.

\[
e(X_i) = P(D_i = 1 | X_i)
\]
Where:

\(D\_i = 1\) if person i receives the treatment.
\(X\_i\) is the vector of all observed pre-treatment covariates for person i (e.g., age, gender, baseline health status).

Think of it like this: if someone has a propensity score of 0.8, it means that based on their observed characteristics, they had an 80% chance of being in the treatment group. A person with a score of 0.1 had only a 10% chance.



This is the theoretical cornerstone that makes propensity scores so powerful.

Theorem (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983): If we correctly specify the propensity score model, then within strata of the propensity score, the distribution of the observed covariates X is independent of treatment status D.

\[
(Y^1, Y^0) \perp D | X \implies (Y^1, Y^0) \perp D | e(X)
\]
In plain language: If you take a treated person and an untreated person who have the exact same propensity score, you can think of them as being “statistically equivalent” on all the observed covariates that went into the score. It’s as if, for that pair of individuals, the treatment was randomly assigned. By conditioning on this single score, we have “balanced” all the observed confounders simultaneously.






Key Assumption: Ignorability & Positivity




Ignorability (or Unconfoundedness): We must assume that we have measured and included all common causes of the treatment and the outcome in our propensity score model. Propensity scores cannot balance unobserved confounders (e.g., genetic factors, motivation).
Positivity (or Overlap): For any set of covariates X, there must be a non-zero probability of being both treated and untreated. \(0 < P(D=1 | X=x) < 1\). If a certain type of person always gets the treatment, we have no one to compare them to.







Let’s make this extremely simple. Imagine we have 6 patients. We want to know if a new drug (D=1) helps reduce blood pressure (Y). We know that age (X) is a confounder: older people have higher blood pressure and are also more likely to get the new drug.

By matching on the propensity score, we’ve created a control group that is “more similar” to the treated group, and our effect estimate is less biased.



Let’s expand our R example to be more realistic. We’ll simulate data where Age and Comorbidity (a measure of baseline health) are confounders. The true treatment effect is 10.
# Load necessary libraries
library(dplyr)
library(MatchIt)
library(WeightIt)
library(cobalt) # For balance checking

# --- 1. Simulate a richer dataset with confounding ---
set.seed(42)
n <- 1000
data <- tibble(
  # Two confounders: Age and a comorbidity score
  X_age = round(runif(n, 40, 75)),
  X_comorbidity = round(runif(n, 0, 5)),
  # Probability of treatment depends on BOTH confounders
  propensity_true = 1 / (1 + exp(-( -4 + 0.05 * X_age + 0.1 * X_comorbidity ))),
  # Treatment status D (1=Treated, 0=Control)
  D = rbinom(n, 1, propensity_true),
  # Outcome Y depends on confounders and treatment. True ATE = 10.
  Y = 50 + 0.5 * X_age + 2 * X_comorbidity + 10 * D + rnorm(n, 0, 5)
)

# --- 2. Estimate propensity scores using logistic regression ---
# The formula D ~ X_age + X_comorbidity means we are modeling the probability
# of receiving treatment D based on a patient's age and comorbidity score.
ps_model <- glm(D ~ X_age + X_comorbidity, data = data, family = "binomial")
data$propensity_est <- predict(ps_model, type = "response")

# --- 3. Implement Propensity Score Matching ---
# The MatchIt package does all the heavy lifting for us.
# method = "nearest" means we're doing 1-to-1 nearest neighbor matching.
# distance = "logit" means we match on the logit of the propensity score, which often works better.
matched_data_obj <- matchit(D ~ X_age + X_comorbidity, data = data,
                            method = "nearest", distance = "logit")

# --- 4. ASSESS BALANCE ---
# This is a critical step! Did the matching work?
# We want to see that the means of the covariates are now similar between
# the treated and control groups in our matched sample.
# A "Love Plot" is a great way to visualize this.
love.plot(matched_data_obj, thresholds = c(m = 0.1), abs = TRUE,
          var.order = "unadjusted",
          title = "Covariate Balance Before and After Matching")
The Love Plot shows the Standardized Mean Difference (SMD) for each covariate before and after matching. An SMD close to 0 indicates good balance. A common rule of thumb is that the absolute SMD should be less than 0.1.
# --- 5. Estimate the Causal Effect from the Matched Data ---
# Extract the new dataset of matched individuals
matched_data <- match.data(matched_data_obj)

# Run a simple regression on the matched data to get the ATE
# This automatically handles the matched pairs correctly.
matched_model <- lm(Y ~ D, data = matched_data, weights = weights)
summary(matched_model) # The coefficient for D is our ATE estimate!


Matching can be inefficient because it discards unmatched control units. IPTW uses all the data, but weights it to create a balanced “pseudo-population.”
The Intuition:

A treated person with a high propensity score (e.g., 0.9) was “very likely” to get the treatment. They are common, so we give them a small weight: weight = 1 / 0.9 = 1.11.
A treated person with a low propensity score (e.g., 0.1) was “unlikely” to get the treatment. They are rare and thus highly informative. We give them a large weight: weight = 1 / 0.1 = 10.
Similarly, untreated people get a weight of 1 / (1 - e(X)).

This weighting scheme creates a new sample where the treatment is no longer associated with the covariates X.
# --- 6. Implement IPTW ---
# The WeightIt package simplifies this process.
# It automatically calculates the weights based on our propensity score model.
weight_obj <- weightit(D ~ X_age + X_comorbidity, data = data, method = "ps")

# Add the weights to our original dataframe
data$iptw <- weight_obj$weights

# --- 7. Estimate the Causal Effect using Weighted Regression ---
# Run a regression on the FULL dataset, but tell it to use the weights.
iptw_model <- lm(Y ~ D, data = data, weights = iptw)
summary(iptw_model) # The coefficient for D is our IPTW ATE estimate.






Motivation: This derivation shows how the simple inverse probability weighting formula mathematically removes confounding bias and isolates the average treatment effect (ATE).
Goal: We want to estimate the ATE, which is defined as \(E[Y^1] - E[Y^0]\).
Derivation for \(E[Y^1]\):

We start with the observed mean for the treated, but we want the population mean. We can write \(E[Y^1]\) using the law of total expectation:

\[
E[Y^1] = E[E[Y^1|X]]
\]

Under the assumption of consistency (\(Y = D \cdot Y^1 + (1-D) \cdot Y^0\)), for people who actually received the treatment (\(D=1\)), their observed outcome \(Y\) is equal to their potential outcome \(Y^1\).

\[
E[Y|D=1, X] = E[Y^1|D=1, X]
\]

Under the assumption of ignorability (\(Y^1 \perp D | X\)), conditioning on X is enough to break the link between treatment and potential outcomes.

\[
E[Y^1|D=1, X] = E[Y^1|X]
\]
Therefore, \(E[Y|D=1, X] = E[Y^1|X]\). We can now express the population mean \(E[Y^1]\) in terms of observed quantities.

Let’s define the propensity score \(e(X) = P(D=1|X)\). We can cleverly rewrite the expectation of the weighted outcome for treated people: \[
E\left[\frac{D \cdot Y}{e(X)}\right] = E\left[ E\left[ \frac{D \cdot Y}{e(X)} \Bigg| X \right] \right] \quad \text{(by Law of Iterated Expectations)}
\]
Let’s focus on the inner expectation. Since \(e(X)\) is a function of \(X\), it can be treated as a constant within this expectation.

\[
E\left[ \frac{D \cdot Y}{e(X)} \Bigg| X \right] = \frac{1}{e(X)} E[D \cdot Y | X]
\]
\(E[D \cdot Y | X] = P(D=1|X)E[Y|D=1,X] + P(D=0|X)E[Y|D=0,X] \cdot 0\)
\[
= e(X) E[Y|D=1,X]
\] 6. Substituting this back in: \[
\frac{1}{e(X)} \cdot e(X) E[Y|D=1,X] = E[Y|D=1,X]
\]

From our earlier steps, we know \(E[Y|D=1,X] = E[Y^1|X]\). So, the inner expectation simplifies to \(E[Y^1|X]\).
Substituting this back into the outer expectation: \[
E\left[\frac{D \cdot Y}{e(X)}\right] = E[E[Y^1|X]] = E[Y^1]
\]

Conclusion: We have shown that the expectation of the inverse-probability-weighted outcome for the treated group is an unbiased estimator for the population average potential outcome under treatment, \(E[Y^1]\). A parallel derivation shows that \(E\left[\frac{(1-D) \cdot Y}{1-e(X)}\right] = E[Y^0]\).
Therefore, the simple IPTW estimator for the ATE is: \[
\widehat{ATE}_{IPTW} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{D_i Y_i}{e(X_i)} - \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{(1-D_i) Y_i}{1-e(X_i)}
\]

Let’s focus on the inner expectation. Since \(e(X)\) is a function of \(X\), it can be treated as a constant within this expectation.

\[
E\left[ \frac{D \cdot Y}{e(X)} \Bigg| X \right] = \frac{1}{e(X)} E[D \cdot Y | X]
\]
\(E[D \cdot Y | X] = P(D=1|X)E[Y|D=1,X] + P(D=0|X)E[Y|D=0,X] \cdot 0\)
\[
= e(X) E[Y|D=1,X]
\] 6. Substituting this back in: \[
\frac{1}{e(X)} \cdot e(X) E[Y|D=1,X] = E[Y|D=1,X]
\]

From our earlier steps, we know \(E[Y|D=1,X] = E[Y^1|X]\). So, the inner expectation simplifies to \(E[Y^1|X]\).
Substituting this back into the outer expectation: \[
E\left[\frac{D \cdot Y}{e(X)}\right] = E[E[Y^1|X]] = E[Y^1]
\]

Conclusion: We have shown that the expectation of the inverse-probability-weighted outcome for the treated group is an unbiased estimator for the population average potential outcome under treatment, \(E[Y^1]\). A parallel derivation shows that \(E\left[\frac{(1-D) \cdot Y}{1-e(X)}\right] = E[Y^0]\).
Therefore, the simple IPTW estimator for the ATE is: \[
\widehat{ATE}_{IPTW} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{D_i Y_i}{e(X_i)} - \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{(1-D_i) Y_i}{1-e(X_i)}
\]

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
So far, we have focused on methods like regression adjustment, matching, and weighting. All these methods share a common, crucial assumption: ignorability. They require us to believe that we have successfully measured and controlled for all common causes of the treatment and the outcome.
But what if we can’t? What if there is a powerful, unmeasured confounder that we simply do not have in our dataset? This could be something like “patient motivation,” “physician skill,” or “innate ability.” In these cases, our previous methods will fail to produce an unbiased causal estimate.
This week, we introduce Instrumental Variables (IV), a brilliant and powerful method for estimating causal effects even in the presence of unmeasured confounding. The core idea is to find a “natural experiment” or a “random nudge” that affects the treatment but is not itself related to the outcome, except through its effect on the treatment.
By the end of this module, you will be able to:

Identify situations where unmeasured confounding makes standard methods inappropriate.
Define an instrumental variable and articulate its three core assumptions.
Explain the intuition behind IV estimation using the Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS) method.
Implement IV estimation in R using the ivreg package.
Understand what the IV method actually estimates: the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE).
Recognize and diagnose the problem of “weak instruments.”

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
section: 🧠 Key Concepts: Hacking Causality with a “Nudge”
text:
🧠 Key Concepts: Hacking Causality with a “Nudge”

The Enduring Problem: Unmeasured Confounding
Let’s consider a classic question: What is the causal effect of completing a college degree (D) on future earnings (Y)?
A simple regression of earnings on education will likely be biased. Why? Because individuals with higher innate ability (U) are both more likely to finish college and more likely to earn more, regardless of their education.
Since “ability” is nearly impossible to measure, it becomes an unmeasured confounder, creating a backdoor path (\(D \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y\)) that we cannot close with standard methods.


The IV Solution: Finding a Clean Pathway
The IV approach seeks to find a variable—the instrument (Z)—that “nudges” people into treatment but is itself unrelated to the confounder.
An instrumental variable is a variable Z that affects the outcome Y only through its effect on the treatment D.
A classic example is using geographic proximity to a college as an instrument for education. People who live closer to a college (Z) may be more likely to attend (D), but where they live is probably not related to their innate ability (U).


The Three Core IV Assumptions
For a variable Z to be a valid instrument, it must satisfy three conditions:

Relevance: The instrument must have a causal effect on the treatment.

\(Cov(Z, D) \neq 0\)
Intuition: Proximity to a college must actually affect the probability that someone attends college. An irrelevant instrument is useless. We can and should test this with data.

Exclusion Restriction: The instrument must affect the outcome only through the treatment. It cannot have a direct effect on the outcome.

Intuition: Living near a college cannot directly increase your earnings. It can only do so by making you more likely to get a degree. This is a strong assumption and cannot be proven with data; it must be justified by theory and domain knowledge.

Exchangeability (or Independence): The instrument must not share any common causes with the outcome. It must be “as-if” randomly assigned with respect to the unmeasured confounders.

\(Cov(Z, U) = 0\)
Intuition: The types of people who live near a college cannot be systematically different (in terms of ability) from those who live far away.








Justifying the IV Assumptions is Key



The validity of an IV analysis rests entirely on the plausibility of these three assumptions. While relevance can be tested, the exclusion restriction and exchangeability are untestable assumptions that you must defend based on institutional knowledge and logical argument.

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
✅ Numerical Example: Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS)
The most common IV estimator is Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS). The intuition is beautiful: we “cleanse” the endogenous treatment variable of its correlation with the unmeasured confounder.
Imagine our goal is to estimate: \(Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D + \epsilon\)
But we know \(D\) is correlated with \(\epsilon\) (because of U).
Stage 1: Isolate the “Clean” Variation in Treatment First, we predict the treatment D using only our instrument Z.
\[
D = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 Z + \nu
\]
The predicted values from this regression, \(\hat{D}\), represent the part of the treatment that is “exogenous”—i.e., the part that is purely driven by our “as-if” random instrument.
Stage 2: Estimate the Causal Effect Second, we regress the outcome Y on the predicted treatment from Stage 1.
\[
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \hat{D} + \epsilon'
\]
Because \(\hat{D}\) is, by construction, uncorrelated with the unmeasured confounder U, the resulting estimate of \(\beta_1\) is our unbiased IV estimate of the causal effect.

A Worked Example in R
Let’s simulate data for the education-earnings example. We’ll set the true causal effect of education to 5 (e.g., $5,000).
# Load necessary libraries
library(dplyr)
library(ivreg)
library(AER) # Contains the dataset we'll use

# --- 1. Simulate data with an unmeasured confounder ---
set.seed(123)
n <- 1000
# Z: Instrument (Proximity to college, 1=close, 0=far)
# U: Unmeasured confounder (Ability)
# D: Treatment (Gets a degree)
# Y: Outcome (Earnings)
data <- tibble(
  Z = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5),
  U = rnorm(n, 0, 1),
  # Treatment depends on the instrument Z and ability U
  D = rbinom(n, 1, pnorm(0.5 * Z + 1.5 * U - 0.5)),
  # Outcome depends on treatment D and ability U. True effect of D is 5.
  Y = 10 + 5 * D + 3 * U + rnorm(n, 0, 2)
)

# --- 2. OLS (Naive) Regression ---
# This is biased by the unmeasured confounder U
ols_model <- lm(Y ~ D, data = data)
summary(ols_model)
# The coefficient on D is ~8.1, which is badly biased upwards from the true value of 5.

# --- 3. IV Regression using 2SLS ---
# The syntax for ivreg is Y ~ treatment | instrument(s)
# It performs both stages for us automatically.
iv_model <- ivreg(Y ~ D | Z, data = data)
summary(iv_model)
# The coefficient on D is now ~4.9, very close to our true effect of 5!

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
section: 📘 IV in the Potential Outcomes Framework: What is the LATE?
text:
📘 IV in the Potential Outcomes Framework: What is the LATE?
The IV estimate is not the Average Treatment Effect (ATE). Instead, it is the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE). To understand this, we need to define four types of people in our population relative to the instrument:

Compliers: These are individuals who take the treatment if encouraged by the instrument, and don’t if they are not. (They comply with the “nudge”).
Always-Takers: These individuals will take the treatment regardless of the instrument’s value.
Never-Takers: These individuals will never take the treatment, regardless of the instrument.
Defiers: These individuals do the opposite of what the instrument encourages. (This group is generally assumed not to exist).

The LATE theorem (Angrist & Imbens, 1994) states that the IV estimate is the average treatment effect only for the compliers.

Concept Check
Let’s use a military draft lottery as an instrument for veteran status to study the effect of military service on health. Who are the “compliers”?
Answer: The compliers are the men who would only serve in the military if they were drafted, but would not volunteer otherwise. The IV estimate gives us the effect of military service only for this specific subgroup, not for the always-takers (volunteers) or never-takers (those who would avoid service even if drafted).







The Problem of Weak Instruments



A “weak instrument” is an instrument that satisfies the exclusion and exchangeability assumptions, but is only weakly correlated with the treatment (the Relevance assumption is weak).

Consequence 1: The IV estimate becomes biased in the direction of the OLS estimate.
Consequence 2: The standard errors of the IV estimate become very large.

Rule of Thumb: In the first stage regression (D ~ Z), check the F-statistic for the significance of the instrument. If the F-statistic is less than 10, you likely have a weak instrument problem.

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
section: 📚 Appendix: Advanced Statistical Derivations and Theory
text:
📚 Appendix: Advanced Statistical Derivations and Theory

📕 Derivation of the Simple IV Estimator
Motivation: This derivation shows how the ratio of two covariances can produce a consistent estimator for the causal effect \(\beta_1\) in the presence of an unmeasured confounder.
The Model: Assume the true structural model is:

\(Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D + U\) (where U is the unmeasured confounder)
\(D = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 Z + V\) (where Z is the instrument)

We assume the key IV property: \(Cov(Z, U) = 0\). Our goal is to estimate \(\beta_1\).

Start with the covariance between the outcome Y and the instrument Z:

\[
Cov(Y, Z) = Cov(\beta_0 + \beta_1 D + U, Z)
\]

Using the properties of covariance, this expands to:

\[
Cov(Y, Z) = Cov(\beta_0, Z) + \beta_1 Cov(D, Z) + Cov(U, Z)
\]

Simplify the terms:

\(Cov(\beta_0, Z) = 0\) (covariance with a constant is zero).
\(Cov(U, Z) = 0\) (this is our crucial exchangeability assumption).

This leaves us with a simple expression:

\[
Cov(Y, Z) = \beta_1 Cov(D, Z)
\]

Solve for our target parameter, \(\beta_1\):

\[
\beta_1 = \frac{Cov(Y, Z)}{Cov(D, Z)}
\]
Conclusion: The true causal effect \(\beta_1\) is the ratio of the “reduced form” effect of the instrument on the outcome (the numerator) to the “first stage” effect of the instrument on the treatment (the denominator). The sample counterparts of these covariances form the simple IV estimator:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{IV} = \frac{\sum (Y_i - \bar{Y})(Z_i - \bar{Z})}{\sum (D_i - \bar{D})(Z_i - \bar{Z})}
\]

title: Week 3: Confounding, Selection Bias, and Colliders
text:
In our last module, we learned the “grammar” of causal inference using Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). Now, we use this grammar to diagnose and understand the primary threats that prevent us from making valid causal claims from observational data: confounding and selection bias.
These concepts are the reasons why well-intentioned analyses can lead to dangerously wrong conclusions. For decades, observational studies suggested that hormone replacement therapy (HRT) protected against heart disease, a conclusion that was later overturned by randomized trials showing it could be harmful. What went wrong? The answer lies in confounding—the women who opted to take HRT were already healthier and had more health-conscious behaviors than those who did not.
By the end of this module, you will be able to:

Define confounding and selection bias using both the potential outcomes and causal graph frameworks.
Identify confounding (open backdoor paths) and selection bias (often caused by conditioning on a collider) in a DAG.
Implement control strategies like stratification and regression to address confounding.
Recognize subtle forms of bias, such as M-bias, and understand why “controlling for everything” can be harmful.
Apply these concepts to critically evaluate the validity of causal claims from observational studies.

title: Week 3: Confounding, Selection Bias, and Colliders
section: Key Concepts: The Villains of Observational Research
text:
Key Concepts: The Villains of Observational Research

1. Confounding: The Hidden Common Cause
Confounding is the most famous threat to causal inference. It occurs when a third variable is associated with both the exposure and the outcome, creating a spurious (non-causal) link between them.
Formal Definition (DAGs): Confounding occurs when there is an unblocked backdoor path between an exposure A and an outcome Y. This path is created by a common cause (C) of A and Y, represented by the “fork” structure: A ← C → Y.
Intuition: Imagine you observe that cities with more ice cream sales (A) also have more drowning deaths (Y). Does ice cream cause drowning? No. A third variable, hot weather (C), is a common cause of both. Hot weather increases ice cream sales and also causes more people to swim (and thus, more drownings). Unless we account for the weather, we will draw a wrong conclusion.
Control Strategies: To eliminate confounding, we must block the backdoor path. The two most common methods are:

Stratification (or Restriction): We analyze the relationship between A and Y within levels of the confounder C. For example, we could compare ice cream sales and drownings only on days with similar temperatures.
Regression Adjustment: We include the confounder C as a covariate in a regression model (e.g., lm(Y ~ A + C)). This statistically “holds C constant.”







✅ Numerical Example 1 (Stratification): The Hypertension Drug



Let’s examine the effect of a new hypertension drug (A) on 1-year mortality (Y), where disease severity (Z) is a confounder. Sicker patients are both more likely to receive the new drug and more likely to die.

The crude risk ratio is (40/100) / (20/100) = 2.0. It appears the new drug doubles the risk of death!
Step 1: Stratify by Severity (Z)
High Severity (Z=1) Stratum-specific RR = (32/80) / (10/20) = 0.4 / 0.5 = 0.8
Low Severity (Z=0) Stratum-specific RR = (8/20) / (10/80) = 0.4 / 0.125 = 3.2. Let’s make this example consistent.

✅ Numerical Example 2 (Regression Adjustment)



Let’s simulate a continuous example in R.
Scenario: We want to estimate the effect of daily minutes of exercise (A) on a continuous health score (Y), but this is confounded by age (Z).
set.seed(123)
n <- 500
age <- runif(n, 20, 70) # Z: Age is a confounder
# A: Exercise decreases with age
exercise <- 120 - 1 * age + rnorm(n, 0, 20)
# Y: Health score decreases with age but increases with exercise (true effect = 0.5)
health_score <- 80 - 0.5 * age + 0.5 * exercise + rnorm(n, 0, 10)

df <- data.frame(health_score, exercise, age)

# Naive (Biased) Model: Ignores the confounder age
naive_model <- lm(health_score ~ exercise, data = df)
summary(naive_model)
#>               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
#> (Intercept)   56.1268     1.3735   40.86   <2e-16 ***
#> exercise       0.0152     0.0189    0.80   0.422

# Adjusted (Unbiased) Model: Controls for age
adjusted_model <- lm(health_score ~ exercise + age, data = df)
summary(adjusted_model)
#>               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
#> (Intercept)   79.6209     2.5020   31.82   <2e-16 ***
#> exercise       0.5147     0.0125   41.24   <2e-16 ***
#> age           -0.4950     0.0255  -19.41   <2e-16 ***
Interpretation: The naive model finds a near-zero, insignificant effect of exercise. This is because younger people exercise more and are healthier, while older people exercise less and are less healthy. The positive effect of exercise is cancelled out by the negative effect of age. Once we control for age in the adjusted model, we recover the true causal effect: each additional minute of exercise increases the health score by 0.51 points.




2. Selection Bias and the Menace of Colliders
Selection bias is a systematic error that occurs when the process of selecting subjects into a study is related to both the exposure and the outcome.
Formal Definition (DAGs): A very common and insidious form of selection bias is collider bias. This occurs when we condition on a collider.
Intuition: Remember, a collider is a variable that is a common effect. Conditioning on it creates a spurious association between its causes. This act of conditioning can be explicit (adding the collider to a regression) or implicit (designing a study where the sample is defined by the collider).






✅ Example: The “Low Birthweight Paradox”



A famous real-world example of collider bias involves smoking and infant mortality.

Exposure A: Maternal Smoking
Outcome Y: Infant Mortality
Unobserved Factor U: Congenital malformations.
Collider C: Low Birthweight (LBW)

The DAG: Smoking (A) can cause LBW (C). Certain congenital defects (U) also cause LBW (C) and strongly increase the risk of infant mortality (Y). The simplified DAG looks like this: A → C ← U → Y.
The Paradox: In the general population, smoking increases infant mortality. However, if researchers restrict their analysis to only low-birthweight babies, they often find that infants of smoking mothers have a lower mortality rate than infants of non-smoking mothers.
The Explanation: This is classic collider bias. We are conditioning on the collider, LBW (C). Among LBW babies, a child of a non-smoker must have another powerful reason for their low birthweight, such as a severe congenital defect (U). A child of a smoker might have LBW simply because their mother smoked. Therefore, within the LBW stratum, maternal smoking becomes spuriously associated with a lower risk of having other, more fatal, problems.




3. M-Bias: The Deceptive Confounder
Controlling for variables that occur before the exposure seems safe, right? Not always. M-bias is a specific form of collider bias that can occur when we condition on a pre-exposure variable that is not a true confounder.
The DAG Structure: Imagine the following structure, which looks like the letter ‘M’. A ← U1 → Z ← U2 → Y

A is the exposure, Y is the outcome.
Z is a pre-exposure covariate we are tempted to control for.
U1 and U2 are unobserved common causes.

The Problem: In this DAG, there is no open backdoor path between A and Y. The path A ← U1 → Z ← U2 → Y is naturally blocked by the collider, Z. The naive association between A and Y is unbiased.
However, if we condition on Z, we unblock the path by opening the collider. This creates a spurious association between A and Y, inducing bias.






The Pitfall of “Kitchen Sink” Regressions



M-bias is a stark warning against the practice of including every available pre-exposure variable in a regression model. A variable is not a confounder just because it is associated with both the exposure and the outcome. It must be a common cause. You must use your substantive knowledge, encoded in a DAG, to decide which variables to adjust for.




Check Your Understanding
You are studying the effect of a new hypertension medication (A) on stroke risk (Y). You build the following DAG based on your knowledge:
A ← Doctor's Preference (U1) → Patient's Zip Code (Z) ← Socioeconomic Status (U2) → Y
A colleague suggests you should control for the patient’s zip code (Z) because it’s associated with both the medication prescribed and stroke risk. What do you say?
##


Answer

You Should Advise against Controlling for Zip Code. In This DAG, Zip Code (Z) is a Collider. It is Caused by the Doctor’s Preferred Hospital Network (U1, Which Influences Prescribing A) and the Patient’s Socioeconomic Status (U2, Which Influences Stroke risk Y). Controlling for Z Would Induce M-bias, Creating a Spurious Association between the Medication and Stroke risk where None Might Exist.



Appendix: Advanced Statistical Derivations and Theory

📕 Motivation: Formalizing the Backdoor Adjustment
In the main text, we used intuition and numerical examples to show that conditioning on confounders gives us the causal effect. The mathematical justification for this comes from the Backdoor Adjustment Formula, which connects the interventional do()-calculus to standard conditional probabilities.
The Goal: We want to estimate \(P(Y=y | do(A=a))\). We can’t observe this directly. The backdoor adjustment formula shows how to compute it from observational data, provided we have measured a set of variables Z that satisfy the backdoor criterion.


📕 Derivation: The Backdoor Adjustment Formula
The formula is:
\[
P(Y=y | do(A=a)) = \sum_{z} P(Y=y | A=a, Z=z) \times P(Z=z)
\]
Let’s walk through a conceptual derivation:

Start with the Goal: We want to know the outcome distribution in a population where everyone has been forced to take exposure level a.
Stratify the Population: We can think of the overall population as being composed of different strata, defined by the levels of our confounders Z. The overall effect is the average of the effects within these strata, weighted by the proportion of the population in each stratum, \(P(Z=z)\).
Estimate the Effect within a Stratum: Within a specific stratum Z=z, all backdoor paths are blocked. This means that the statistical association is equal to the causal effect. So, for the subgroup where Z=z, the outcome distribution under the intervention do(A=a) is just the observed conditional probability \(P(Y=y | A=a, Z=z)\).

Annotation: This is the key step. Because Z satisfies the backdoor criterion, the causal link A → Y is the only thing connecting them within a level of Z. So, P(Y|do(A), Z) = P(Y|A, Z).

Average Across Strata: To get the effect for the whole population, we average the stratum-specific effects, weighting each by that stratum’s prevalence, \(P(Z=z)\). This gives us the formula above.

This formula is the mathematical engine behind control strategies like stratification and regression adjustment. It formally shows how conditioning on a valid set of confounders allows us to estimate a causal effect from observational data.

title: Week 9: Time-Varying Treatments and Marginal Structural Models
text: We are now moving into one of the most powerful and modern areas of applied causal inference: handling treatments that change over time. In the real world, medical treatments, social policies, and environmental exposures are not static. Doctors adjust medications based on patient progress, governments modify programs, and individuals change behaviors. Our methods must be ableto handle this dynamic reality. This week, we introduce the framework and methods to do just that.

title: Week 9: Time-Varying Treatments and Marginal Structural Models
text:
🎯 Learning Objectives & Motivation
Our goal is to understand how to estimate the causal effects of treatment strategies or regimes over time. Standard methods that we’ve learned, like regression adjustment or single-time-point propensity scores, will fail us here. This failure is not a minor detail; it can lead to qualitatively wrong conclusions.
By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:

Define and identify time-varying confounding in a real-world scenario.
Explain, using a DAG, precisely why standard regression adjustment is biased in this context.
Distinguish between a marginal model and a conditional model, and articulate why we need the former.
Describe the structure and causal interpretation of a Marginal Structural Model (MSM).
Calculate and interpret stabilized Inverse Probability of Treatment Weights (IPTW).
Implement an MSM analysis in R and critically assess its assumptions.
Explain the logic of G-computation as an alternative to IPTW.


The Motivation: Two Scenarios
Let’s ground our discussion in two motivating public health examples.
Scenario 1: HIV Treatment 💊 A patient with HIV is followed for several years. Every six months, their doctor:

Measures their CD4 count (L), a marker of immune system health.
Decides whether to initiate or continue potent antiretroviral therapy (ART) (A).
The final outcome of interest is long-term survival (Y).

The clinical reality is that a low CD4 count (L) today makes a doctor more likely to prescribe ART (A) at the next visit. However, ART (A) taken in the past is intended to increase the CD4 count (L) in the future. The CD4 count is also a strong predictor of survival (Y). This creates a feedback loop that is analytically challenging.
Scenario 2: Asthma and Air Pollution 💨 A pediatric cohort study follows children with asthma. Every month:

Researchers measure the ambient air pollution (A) level in the child’s neighborhood (the “exposure” or “treatment”).
Doctors record the child’s current symptom severity (L), such as frequency of wheezing. Based on this, they might prescribe or adjust the dose of a rescue inhaler.
The outcome (Y) is the number of hospitalizations over the study period.

High air pollution (A) in one month likely worsens symptoms (L) in the next. Severe symptoms (L) are a primary reason for both hospitalization (Y) and for doctors to prescribe more aggressive medication. The medication itself might be considered another time-varying treatment. For simplicity, let’s focus on air pollution (A) as the exposure and symptoms (L) as the key time-varying factor.

title: Week 9: Time-Varying Treatments and Marginal Structural Models
section: 🧠 A Deeper Dive into Time-Varying Confounding
text:
🧠 A Deeper Dive into Time-Varying Confounding
The central challenge in both scenarios is time-varying confounding. Let’s formally define it and see it on a DAG.

A time-varying confounder is a variable that varies over time and is a common cause of both future exposure/treatment and the outcome. The critical problem arises when this confounder is also affected by past exposure/treatment.

Let’s draw a simplified two-time-point DAG that represents this structure.

\(A₀, A₁\): Exposure/Treatment at time 0 and 1.
\(L₀, L₁\): Confounder measured at time 0 and 1.
\(Y\): The final outcome.


graph LR
    subgraph Time 0
        L0[L₀: Baseline Confounder]
        A0[A₀: Treatment]
    end

    subgraph Time 1
        L1[L₁: Time-Varying Confounder]
        A1[A₁: Treatment]
    end

    subgraph Outcome
        Y[Y: Final Outcome]
    end

    %% Causal Paths
    L0 --> A0
    L0 --> L1
    A0 --> L1
    A0 --> A1
    L1 --> A1
    L1 --> Y
    A1 --> Y

    %% Optional direct path for completeness
    A0 --> Y




graph LR
    subgraph Time 0
        L0[L₀: Baseline Confounder]
        A0[A₀: Treatment]
    end

    subgraph Time 1
        L1[L₁: Time-Varying Confounder]
        A1[A₁: Treatment]
    end

    subgraph Outcome
        Y[Y: Final Outcome]
    end

    %% Causal Paths
    L0 --> A0
    L0 --> L1
    A0 --> L1
    A0 --> A1
    L1 --> A1
    L1 --> Y
    A1 --> Y

    %% Optional direct path for completeness
    A0 --> Y






Let’s trace the paths to see the problem:

Confounding of A₁: There is a backdoor path from \(A₁\) to \(Y\): \(A₁ \leftarrow L₁ \rightarrow Y\). To get the causal effect of \(A₁\), we must block this path by conditioning on \(L₁\). This is standard confounding control.
Mediation of A₀: There is a causal path from \(A₀\) to \(Y\): \(A₀ \rightarrow L₁ \rightarrow Y\). This path represents a mechanism by which the initial treatment works: it improves the intermediate health state L₁, which in turn improves the final outcome \(Y\).


The Analytical Trap
If we use a standard regression model (e.g., a generalized linear model) like \(g(E[Y]) = β₀ + β₁A₀ + β₂A₁ + β₃L₀ + β₄L₁\), we are conditioning on \(L₁\).

The Good: Conditioning on L₁ blocks the backdoor path \(A₁ \leftarrow L₁ \rightarrow Y\), controlling for confounding of the A₁-Y relationship. ✅
The Bad: Conditioning on L₁ also blocks the causal path \(A₀ \rightarrow L₁ \rightarrow Y\). This means our estimate β₁ for the effect of A₀ is no longer the total causal effect; it’s only the effect not mediated through L₁. This is a form of overadjustment bias.

Furthermore, and more subtly, L₁ is a collider on the path \(A₀ \rightarrow L₁ \leftarrow \text{U} \rightarrow Y\) where U represents all unmeasured common causes of L₁ and Y. Conditioning on a collider opens the path between the two variables it connects. In this case, conditioning on L₁ can induce a spurious association between A₀ and Y, biasing the estimate for A₀.
You are caught in a statistical Catch-22. You must adjust for L₁ to deal with confounding for A₁, but doing so biases your estimate for A₀. This is why we need a different approach.

title: Week 9: Time-Varying Treatments and Marginal Structural Models
section: 🧠 Key Concept: Marginal vs. Conditional Models
text:
🧠 Key Concept: Marginal vs. Conditional Models
The model \(Y \sim A₀ + A₁ + L₀ + L₁\) is a conditional model. It estimates the effect of A₁ conditional on a fixed level of L₁. This answers a question like: “Among patients who all have a CD4 count of 250, what is the effect of starting ART?” This is a valid, but very specific, scientific question.
Often, we want to know the answer to a more high-level policy question: “What is the overall effect of a policy of ‘starting ART as soon as CD4 drops below 350’ compared to a policy of ‘waiting until CD4 drops below 200’, for the entire population?” This is a marginal question. It averages over all the different levels of the confounders L.
A Marginal Structural Model (MSM) is a model for a marginal causal effect. It models the potential outcome under a given treatment history, without conditioning on the intermediate time-varying confounders.
A simple linear MSM is:
\[
E[Y(\bar{a})] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 a_0 + \beta_2 a_1
\]

\(Y(\bar{a})\) is the potential outcome if a subject were to receive the entire treatment history \(\bar{a} = (a_0, a_1)\).
\(\beta_1\) is the average causal effect of treatment at time 0 on Y.
\(\beta_2\) is the average causal effect of treatment at time 1 on Y, having also received a₀.

This model is “marginal” because \(L₁\) is not in it. The challenge is to estimate the \(\beta\)s when our observed data is plagued by the time-varying confounding involving \(L₁\).

title: Week 9: Time-Varying Treatments and Marginal Structural Models
section: ⚙️ Method 1: Inverse Probability of Treatment Weighting (IPTW)
text:
⚙️ Method 1: Inverse Probability of Treatment Weighting (IPTW)
The magic of MSMs is in their estimation. We use Inverse Probability of Treatment Weighting (IPTW) to create a “pseudo-population” in which the confounding link between the treatment and the time-varying confounders is broken.

Intuition: Re-weighting a Biased Sample
Imagine you’re conducting a political poll but your phone survey accidentally reaches 70% seniors and 30% young people, while the true population is \(50/50\). To get an unbiased estimate of the overall opinion, you would down-weight each senior’s response and up-weight each young person’s response.
IPTW does the same thing, but for confounding. In our observed data, people with “bad” values of \(L\) (low CD4 count) are more likely to get treated. This is not a random sample. We can give a “low” weight to treated people with bad \(L\) values (since we over-sampled them) and a “high” weight to untreated people with bad \(L\) values (since we under-sampled them). After re-weighting, in the pseudo-population, a person’s L value no longer predicts whether they get the treatment. The confounding is removed.


Calculating Stabilized Weights
To avoid issues with extreme weights, we use stabilized weights. The weight for each individual \(i\) is a product over all time points \(k\).
The stabilized weight \(sw_i\) is:
\[
sw_i = \prod_{k=0}^{K} \frac{P(A_{ik} = a_{ik} | \bar{A}_{i,k-1}, L_0)}{P(A_{ik} = a_{ik} | \bar{A}_{i,k-1}, \bar{L}_{ik})}
\]
Let’s break this down:

The Product \(\prod_{k=0}^{K}\): The weight is cumulative. A person’s final weight is the product of their weights from each time point. This reflects the accumulating probability of their entire treatment journey.
The Denominator \(P(A_{ik} = a_{ik} | \bar{A}_{i,k-1}, \bar{L}_{ik})\): This is the probability of receiving the treatment \(a_{ik}\) that person i actually received at time k, given their entire past (past treatments \(\bar{A}_{i,k-1}\) and full confounder history \(\bar{L}_{ik}\)). This is the source of the confounding. We estimate this for each time point, typically with a logistic regression.
The Numerator \(P(A_{ik} = a_{ik} | \bar{A}_{i,k-1}, L_0)\): This is the probability of receiving treatment \(a_{ik}\) given their past treatments and only baseline confounders \(L_0\). Because it doesn’t depend on the time-varying confounders \(L_k\) (for \(k>0\)), it “stabilizes” the weights, pulling them closer to 1 and reducing variance.

The Estimation Procedure:

Fit Denominator Models: For each time \(k\), fit a model for \(P(A_k | \bar{A}_{k-1}, \bar{L}_k)\). (e.g., glm(A1 ~ A0 + L0 + L1, family=binomial))
Fit Numerator Models: For each time \(k\), fit a model for \(P(A_k | \bar{A}_{k-1}, L_0)\). (e.g., glm(A1 ~ A0 + L0, family=binomial))
Predict Probabilities: For each person at each time point, predict the probabilities from both models.
Calculate Weights: For each person, calculate their final weight \(sw_i\) by multiplying the ratios of these probabilities across time.
Fit Weighted MSM: Fit the final marginal model (lm(Y ~ A0 + A1, weights = sw)) using a procedure that accepts weights (like lm or geeglm from the geepack package for robust standard errors). The coefficients from this model are your causal effect estimates.







Assumptions for MSMs with IPTW




Sequential Exchangeability (No Unmeasured Confounding): Conditional on the observed past, the treatment at time k is essentially random. This is the most important and untestable assumption.
Positivity: Everyone, no matter their history, must have a non-zero probability of receiving every level of treatment. \(0 < P(A_k=a_k | \bar{L}_k, \bar{A}_{k-1}) < 1\).
Consistency: An individual’s observed outcome is their potential outcome corresponding to the treatment history they actually received.
Correct Model Specification: The models used to estimate the probabilities for the weights must be correctly specified.





✅ A Worked Example in R
Let’s simulate some data that follows our HIV scenario and apply the method.

title: Week 9: Time-Varying Treatments and Marginal Structural Models
text:
⚙️ Method 2: G-Computation (The G-Formula)
G-computation is a powerful alternative to IPTW. Instead of re-weighting the population, it uses a modeling-based approach to simulate what would have happened under different treatment strategies. It is sometimes called “standardization” extended to the time-varying case.

Conceptual Steps for G-Computation

Model the World Sequentially: Fit a series of regression models for each time-varying factor.

Model 1: \(L₁ ~ A₀ + L₀\) (How the confounder evolves)
Model 2: \(Y ~ A₁ + L₁ + A₀ + L₀\) (How the outcome is generated)
(Note: In a real analysis, you would also need a model for A₀ and A₁ to fully specify the system, but for outcome simulation, these two are key).

Simulate Potential Outcomes under a Fixed Policy:

Policy 1: Never Treat (\(a_0=0, a_1=0\)):

Start with your original dataset (L₀).
Set \(A_0 = 0\) for everyone.
Use Model 1 to predict a potential value of \(L_1(0)\) for everyone.
Set \(A_1 = 0\) for everyone.
Use Model 2 to predict a potential outcome \(Y(0,0)\) for everyone, using their observed \(L_0\) and their simulated \(L_1(0)\).
The average of all these \(Y(0,0)\) predictions is \(E[Y(0,0)]\).

Policy 2: Always Treat (\(a_0=1, a_1=1\)):

Repeat the process, but now force \(A_0=1\) and \(A_1=1\) at the relevant steps. This will generate \(E[Y(1,1)]\).


Calculate Causal Effect: The average causal effect is the difference: \(ATE = E[Y(1,1)] - E[Y(0,0)]\).

G-computation is powerful but carries the heavy burden of requiring correctly specified parametric models for the entire data-generating process. Any misspecification can lead to bias.

title: Week 9: Time-Varying Treatments and Marginal Structural Models
section: 📚 Appendix: Advanced Statistical Derivations and Theory
text:
📚 Appendix: Advanced Statistical Derivations and Theory

Formal Justification for IPTW
Let’s briefly sketch why IPTW works. The goal is to show that in the pseudo-population created by the weights, treatment \(A\) and the confounders \(L\) are independent. We’ll use unstabilized weights (\(w_i = 1 / f(a_i | l_i)\)) for simplicity.
We want to show that the weighted expectation \(E_w[g(L) | A=1]\) is equal to the marginal expectation \(E[g(L)]\), for any function \(g\) of the confounders \(L\). This would mean L has the same distribution among the treated as it does in the total population, implying independence.
\[
E_w[g(L) | A=1] = \frac{E[ \frac{I(A=1)}{f(A=1|L)} g(L) ]}{E[ \frac{I(A=1)}{f(A=1|L)} ]}
\]
Let’s look at the numerator. By the law of iterated expectations (\(E[X] = E[E[X|Z]]\)), we can condition on \(L\).
\[
E \left[ \frac{I(A=1)}{f(A=1|L)} g(L) \right] = E \left\{ E \left[ \left. \frac{I(A=1)}{f(A=1|L)} g(L) \right| L \right] \right\}
\]
Inside the inner expectation, \(g(L)\) and \(f(A=1|L)\) are constants with respect to \(A\).
\[
= E \left\{ \frac{g(L)}{f(A=1|L)} E[I(A=1)|L] \right\}
\]
By definition, \(E[I(A=1)|L] = P(A=1|L) = f(A=1|L)\). So, the terms cancel:
\[
= E \left\{ \frac{g(L)}{f(A=1|L)} f(A=1|L) \right\} = E[g(L)]
\]
A similar calculation shows the denominator equals \(P(A=1)\). Therefore,
\[
E_w[g(L) | A=1] = \frac{E[g(L)]}{P(A=1)}
\]
Wait, this is not quite \(E[g(L)]\). There is a nuance here in the formal derivation for a continuous variable versus a discrete sum. The key insight is that the weighting scheme effectively transforms the joint distribution \(f(y,a,l)\) into a new distribution \(f_w(y,a,l) \propto y \cdot f(y|a,l)f(a)f(l)\) where \(a\) and \(l\) are independent. This relies on the assumption of sequential exchangeability allowing us to factor the joint distribution correctly. The stabilized weights perform a similar function while being more statistically efficient.

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
Step 1: Calculate the First Stage The first stage measures how much the instrument affects treatment probability: \[
\text{First Stage} = P(A=1|Z=1) - P(A=1|Z=0) = 0.50 - 0.40 = 0.10
\]
Step 2: Calculate the Reduced Form The reduced form measures the instrument’s total effect on the outcome: \[
\text{Reduced Form} = E[Y|Z=1] - E[Y|Z=0] = 48 - 45 = 3
\] Step 3: Calculate the IV Estimate The IV estimate is the ratio of reduced form to first stage: \[
\hat{\beta}_1^{IV} = \frac{\text{Reduced Form}}{\text{First Stage}} = \frac{3}{0.10} = 30
\]
Interpretation: Among individuals whose college attendance was influenced by their birth quarter, completing college increases annual earnings by $30,000 on average.
This notation recognizes that the instrument affects treatment choice, and treatment choice affects outcomes. We observe:
Monotonicity is often plausible. For example, if distance to college is our instrument, it’s reasonable that distance never increases someone’s probability of attending college.

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
📘 9.1 What is an Instrument?
Instrumental Variables (IV) represents one of the most powerful yet challenging methods in causal inference. When we cannot conduct a randomized experiment and face the dreaded problem of unobserved confounding, IV offers a potential path forward by exploiting “natural experiments” in observational data.

The Core Problem: Unobserved Confounding
In many real-world scenarios, we cannot assume that all confounders have been measured and controlled for. Consider these examples:

Education and earnings: Unmeasured ability affects both schooling decisions and future income
Hospital quality and patient outcomes: Sicker patients may systematically choose certain hospitals
Treatment adherence and health: Patient motivation influences both medication compliance and health behaviors

Traditional methods like regression adjustment or matching fail when important confounders remain unobserved. This is where instrumental variables shine.


Formal Definition of an Instrumental Variable
An instrumental variable \(Z\) is a variable that enables causal identification of the effect of treatment \(A\) on outcome \(Y\) by satisfying three fundamental assumptions:

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
The Three IV Assumptions

Relevance (Non-zero association): \(Z\) is statistically associated with treatment \(A\)

\[
\text{Cov}(Z, A) \neq 0
\]

Exclusion Restriction (No direct effect): \(Z\) affects outcome \(Y\) only through its effect on treatment \(A\)

\[
Z \perp Y | A, U
\]
where \(U\) represents unmeasured confounders

Exchangeability (No confounding of instrument): \(Z\) is independent of all unmeasured confounders \(U\)

\[
Z \perp U
\]

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
section: 🧠 9.2 No Nonparametric Identification of the ATE
text:
🧠 9.2 No Nonparametric Identification of the ATE
This section addresses one of the most important and often misunderstood limitations of instrumental variables: IV cannot nonparametrically identify the population Average Treatment Effect (ATE) in general settings.

What Do We Mean by “Nonparametric Identification”?
Nonparametric identification means we can recover a causal parameter without making strong functional form assumptions (like linearity). Methods like randomization or backdoor adjustment can nonparametrically identify the ATE - the average effect of treatment for the entire population.


The Fundamental IV Limitation
Instrumental variables face an inherent limitation: they only provide information about individuals whose treatment decisions are affected by the instrument. We learn nothing about treatment effects for people who would make the same treatment choice regardless of the instrument value.

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
The Information Gap

What IV tells us: Treatment effects for people influenced by the instrument
What IV doesn’t tell us: Treatment effects for people unaffected by the instrument
What we want: Treatment effects for the entire population (ATE)

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
Interpretation
The IV estimand: \[
\text{IV Estimand} = \frac{E[Y|Z=1] - E[Y|Z=0]}{E[A|Z=1] - E[A|Z=0]}
\]
is the Wald estimator for the causal effect of a treatment (A) on an outcome (Y) using an instrumental variable (Z).

Interpretation:

The numerator, (\(E[Y|Z=1] - E[Y|Z=0]\)), is the difference in average outcomes between groups defined by the instrument.
The denominator, (\(E[A|Z=1] - E[A|Z=0]\)), is the difference in average treatment rates between those same groups.



Causal Meaning:
This ratio estimates the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE): the average causal effect of (A) on (Y) for individuals whose treatment status is changed by the instrument (Z) (the “compliers”). It is valid under the standard IV assumptions: relevance, exclusion restriction, and exchangeability (plus monotonicity for LATE).


In summary:
The IV estimand isolates the causal effect of the treatment by leveraging exogenous variation in treatment induced by the instrument, thus overcoming unmeasured confounding. It tells us the effect of treatment for those whose treatment status is actually influenced by the instrument.






When IV Can Identify ATE



IV can identify the population ATE under special circumstances:

Homogeneous effects: Everyone has the same treatment effect
Complete compliance: Everyone’s treatment is affected by the instrument
Representative compliers: Those affected by the instrument are representative of the population





The Trade-off: Bias vs. Assumptions
This limitation reflects a fundamental trade-off in causal inference:

Backdoor methods: Can identify ATE but require “no unobserved confounders”
IV methods: Can handle unobserved confounders but typically identify Local ATE

Neither assumption is necessarily better - the choice depends on which is more plausible in your specific application.

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
✅ 9.3 Warm-Up: Binary Linear Setting
Let’s start our technical journey with the simplest possible IV setting: binary instrument, binary treatment, and linear relationships. This serves as our foundation before tackling more complex scenarios.

The Setup
Consider the following simple system:

\(Z \in \{0,1\}\): Binary instrumental variable
\(A \in \{0,1\}\): Binary treatment variable
\(Y\): Continuous outcome
\(U\): Unobserved confounder affecting both \(A\) and \(Y\)



The Structural Model
We can represent this system with two equations:
Treatment equation (First stage): \[
A = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 Z + \gamma_1 U + \epsilon_A
\]
Outcome equation (Second stage): \[
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 A + \gamma_2 U + \epsilon_Y
\]
The parameter of interest is \(\beta_1\) - the causal effect of treatment on outcome.


The Problem with OLS
If we simply regress \(Y\) on \(A\), we get: \[
\hat{\beta}_1^{OLS} = \beta_1 + \gamma_2 \frac{\text{Cov}(A,U)}{\text{Var}(A)}
\]
This is biased whenever treatment and the unobserved confounder are correlated (\(\text{Cov}(A,U) \neq 0\)).


The IV Solution: Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS)
IV solves this by using the instrument to create “clean” variation in treatment:
Stage 1: Predict treatment using only the instrument \[
\hat{A} = \hat{\alpha}_0 + \hat{\alpha}_1 Z
\]
Stage 2: Regress outcome on predicted treatment
\[
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \hat{A} + \epsilon
\]


The IV Formula in Binary Case
In the binary setting, the IV estimator has a particularly clean form: \[
\hat{\beta}_1^{IV} = \frac{E[Y|Z=1]-E[Y|Z=0]}{E[A|Z=1]-E[A|Z=0]} = \frac{\text{Reduced Form}}{\text{First Stage}}
\]
This is the Wald estimator - the ratio of the instrument’s effect on the outcome to the instrument’s effect on treatment.


Step-by-Step Numerical Example

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
College Education and Earnings
Let’s study the effect of college completion on annual earnings using quarter of birth as an instrument.
Setting:

\(Z\): Born in Q4 (1) vs. other quarters (0)
\(A\): College degree (1) vs. no degree (0)
\(Y\): Annual earnings (in thousands of dollars)

Observed Data Summary (n = 1,000):



Birth Quarter
College Rate
Avg Earnings
Sample Size

40%

750

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
Code Explanation

The true causal effect is 25 (coefficient on A in outcome equation)
